ABSTRACT: Confinement of hydrocarbons in nanoscale pockets and pores provides tunable capability for controlling molecules in catalysts, sorbents, and membranes for reaction and separation applications. While computation of the enthalpic interactions of hydrocarbons in confined spaces has improved, understanding and predicting the entropy of confined molecules remains a challenge. Here we show, using a set of nine aluminosilicate zeolite frameworks with broad variation in pore and cavity structure, that the entropy of adsorption can be predicted as a linear combination of rotational and translational entropy. The extent of entropy lost upon adsorption is predicted using only a single material descriptor, the occupiable volume ( $ V_{occ} $). Predictive capability of confined molecular entropy permits an understanding of the relation with adsorption enthalpy, the ability to computationally screen microporous materials, and an understanding of the role of confinement on the kinetics of molecules in confined spaces.

On the basis of this shape-selective feature , highly effective molecular separations and selective catalytic conversions can be achieved within zeolitic structures that are difficult to accomplish with other materials and/or techniques . $ ^ { 1-3 } $ So far, several shape-selectivity mechanisms have been elucidated and applications identified. $ ^{2-18} $ In common molecular sieving, bulky molecules adsorb preferentially over bulkier species as a result of steric constraints imposed by the zeolites' framework, e.g., linear alkane molecules compared to branched isomers. $ ^{19-23} $ Besides this common adsorption competition based on molecular bulkiness, the reverse phenomenon can also occur, i.e., competitive adsorption in favor of the bulkier species. This zeolite with IZA code MWW is a relatively new synthetic material that has an unusual and quite complex pore structure. $ ^{35} $ Its framework is composed of two independent pore systems. The enthalpy and the entropy contributions to the Gibbs free energies were calculated at T = 298 K and partial pressure of 1 atm (101325 Pa). The enthalpy (H) of gas-phase pyridine and acetonitrile molecules is defined as the sum of total electronic energy ( $ E_{el} $), internal vibrational energy ( $ E_{v} $), zero-point vibrational energy (ZPVE), as well as the rotational and translational contributions to the internal energy: $ H = E_{el} + E_{v} + ZPVE + E_{R} + E_{t} $. The corresponding calculated entropies (S) includes translational, ( $ S_{t} $) vibrational, ( $ S_{v} $) and rotational ( $ S_{r} $) degrees of freedom: $ S = S_{t} + S_{v} + S_{r} $. All the considered systems are in singlet state, thus the electronic contribution to the entropy is zero. 1.2.1. Framework dynamics. The first attempts to describe guest-induced flexibility in zeolites were done using molecular dynamics simulations. $ ^{79-82} $ Rigid zeolitic force fields were dynamically modified using transition state theory to include lattice flexibility, and the results obtained by these models were in good agreement with experimental data. $ ^{79-81,83,84} $ It was shown that framework flexibility in silicalite-1 (MFI-type framework) is responsible for the adsorption of large molecules such as isobutane and heptane with inflection behavior at high loadings, $ ^{80} $ while enhanced self-diffusivity at low loadings of short alkanes (i.e. methane and n-butane) was observed. $ ^{81} $ Framework flexibility is also crucial for aromatics adsorption on MFI zeolite, especially at high pressures. $ ^{84,85} $ While the use of rigid zeolitic models led to the underestimation of the aromatics adsorption in MFI zeolite by a factor of two, $ ^{84,85} $ the use of flexible models to simulate diffusion coefficients of various alkanes in silicalite-1 zeolite resulted in a convergence of experimental and theoretical values. $ ^{86} $ Recently by using in situ integrated differential phase contrast scanning transmission electron microscopy (iDPC-STEM) while adsorbing benzene molecules on MFI zeolite, Xiong et al. showed that the MFI structure goes through severe deformations giving another proof of guest-induced flexibility in zeolites (see Fig. 4). $ ^{87} $

2.4.4. Trapdoor. Traditional diﬀusion models primarily consider two types of interactions: those between guest molecules (guest–guest) and those between guest molecules and the zeolite framework (guest–host). However, when cations are present in the zeolite structure, a third interaction—involving guest molecules, the framework, and cations (guest–host-cation)—must also be accounted for. A striking example of such ternary interactions is the well-known ‘‘molecular trapdoor’’. This phenomenon, also referred to as the ‘‘gating effect’’, describes a unique molecular sieving mechanism in certain zeolites and related porous materi- als. Here, extra-framework cations function as dynamic gate- keepers at pore apertures, selectively controlling molecular diffusion to achieve highly discriminative adsorption and separation.9,147,187 To date, ‘‘trapdoor’’ has been observed in several zeolites, including RHO (DNL-6),188–190 CHA (SAPO-34, SSZ-13),147,191,192 MWF (ZSM-25),149,193 HEU (Clinoptilolite),194

descriptor_candidates.name: confined_vol_ratio_d
descriptor_candidates.hypothesis: Hypothesis 1 (occupiable-volume confinement mechanism): The fraction of gas-phase entropy retained upon adsorption, s_ads/s_gas, decreases systematically with the ratio of occupiable pore volume per gram (AV) to molecular volume (Vol), because tighter packing of the guest shape against pore walls suppresses translational freedom. A descriptor built from log(AV/Vol) should reduce entropy-loss MAE relative to a model that already contains the 14 inputs as raw network features, because the network must otherwise learn this multiplicative scaling nonlocally.
descriptor_candidates.rationale: Evidence E01/E03 (pmc6161062) report that entropy loss upon adsorption correlates with occupiable volume and that adsorbed entropy never exceeds gas-phase entropy; confinement restricts translational degrees of freedom. Source evidence: V_occ as single material descriptor (E03). Inference: expressing the ratio AV/Vol (pore volume to molecular volume) compresses the confinement mechanism into one monotonic feature.
descriptor_candidates.falsification_criteria: Adding log(AV*1e6/Vol) as a nonlinear re-expression fails to reduce MAE of entropy loss/R by a pre-specified margin (e.g., <= 0) across cross-validation folds, or the sign of the fitted response to this descriptor is non-monotonic, indicating volume-ratio confinement does not govern s_ads/s_gas for this dataset.

descriptor_candidates.name: shape_elongation_d
descriptor_candidates.hypothesis: Hypothesis 2 (molecular shape-anisotropy mechanism): At fixed pore volume, elongated and anisotropic molecules lose more entropy upon adsorption in channel-type zeolites because rotational freedom about the long axis is preferentially retained while other rotations are frozen. A combined descriptor of molecular aspect (SPAN/GeDi) and moment-of-memory anisotropy (PMI2/PMI1) improves prediction of entropy loss/R beyond volume alone.
descriptor_candidates.rationale: Evidence E01 notes that the relation between molecular shape and confinement entropy (Delta S_conf) remains undetermined and that entropy loss differs by framework (TON largest, FAU smallest); evidence E05 shows shape selectivity arises from steric matching of molecular bulk to pore geometry. Source evidence: shape-dependent entropy partitioning into rotational modes (E01). Inference: anisotropy ratios SPAN/GeDi and PMI2/PMI1 proxy the number of accessible rotational degrees of freedom lost in channel confinement.
descriptor_candidates.falsification_criteria: If the shape-anisotropy descriptor's partial contribution is statistically indistinguishable from zero (e.g., MAE change within noise of fold variance) or its effect does not differ between channel-type (TON, MFI, MOR) and cage-type (FAU, CHA) frameworks in residual analysis, the rotational-anisotropy mechanism is falsified for this dataset.

descriptor_candidates.name: aperture_density_d
descriptor_candidates.hypothesis: Hypothesis 3 (pore-aperture accessibility mechanism): Entropy loss is governed not by total pore volume but by the accessibility of confinement sites, proxied by the interplay of largest free sphere diameters of the pore (lsd_p) and framework (lsd_f) with accessible surface area density (ASA relative to AV). Materials with apertures only slightly smaller than the framework free sphere and low surface-area-to-volume density (cage-like, FAU-like) retain more entropy; tight, channel-like geometries (TON-like) lose more. This descriptor should reduce MAE of entropy loss/R especially for adsorbates whose molecular dimension (PBF) is near the aperture.
descriptor_candidates.rationale: Evidence E01 shows framework-dependent entropy loss (TON largest, FAU smallest), implying topology/aperture geometry, not volume alone, controls confinement entropy; E06 shows translational and rotational degrees of freedom are reduced by fixed factors upon confinement in cavities. Source evidence: framework-specific entropy losses and reduced rotational/translational freedom in cavities (E01, E06). Inference: lsd_p vs lsd_f contrast proxies aperture tightness; ASA/AV proxies the fraction of confined wall-adjacent sites; the exponential term captures the sharp threshold behavior of molecular sieving (E07).
descriptor_candidates.falsification_criteria: The descriptor fails if (a) including it does not improve MAE of entropy loss/R over the volume-ratio descriptor of Hypothesis 1 (i.e., no incremental information beyond total confinement volume), or (b) the fitted dependence on lsd_p/lsd_f is flat across frameworks, indicating aperture accessibility geometry does not modulate entropy loss independently of occupiable volume.

descriptor_candidates.name: wall_proximity_d
descriptor_candidates.hypothesis: Hypothesis 2 (surface-area-normalized wall-proximity mechanism): Beyond total occupiable volume (Hypothesis 1), the entropy fraction retained upon adsorption, s_ads/s_gas, increases with the amount of surface accessible per unit pore volume relative to the molecular radius of gyration proxy (PBF). Molecules sitting close to many wall segments lose configurational entropy through frustrated rotation/vibration; a large accessible surface per pore volume combined with a small PBF maximizes wall contact and thus entropy loss. A single log ratio compressing LabuteASA/Vol and PBF should add information not locally learnable from the raw 14 features.
descriptor_candidates.rationale: Source evidence: E01 shows entropy loss differs systematically across frameworks (TON largest, FAU smallest), implying wall-contact geometry beyond volume controls Delta S_ads; E06 shows translational and rotational entropies are reduced by fixed factors when molecules are constrained in cavities. Inference: accessible surface area density (LabuteASA/AV) times molecular proximity (1/(PBF)) proxies the fraction of the molecule's configurational phase space frozen by wall contact; the log form gives a monotonic, scale-free feature.
descriptor_candidates.falsification_criteria: Adding this descriptor to the model containing the 14 raw inputs and log(AV/Vol) fails to reduce MAE of entropy loss/R below the round-1 best (0.5541) across cross-validation folds, or the fitted response has the wrong sign (entropy loss decreases with increasing surface-area density), falsifying the wall-proximity mechanism for this dataset.

descriptor_candidates.name: packing_tightness_d
descriptor_candidates.hypothesis: Hypothesis 3 (molecular-fit tightness mechanism): Entropy loss depends on how snugly the molecule fills the largest confining cavity, not on cavity size alone. The ratio of molecular volume (Vol) to the cube of the pore limiting diameter (lsd_p^3) measures how much of the largest free sphere the molecule occupies; molecules filling a large fraction of the cavity lose more rotational/translational entropy. Combined with a mass-per-volume term sqrt(Vol/MW) (a compactness proxy: compact heavy molecules lose more entropy per mode than elongated light ones at the same volume), this descriptor should improve prediction of entropy loss/R beyond the retained volume-ratio descriptor.
descriptor_candidates.rationale: Source evidence: E01 reports framework-specific entropy losses and that shape-confinement relations remain undetermined; E05 shows steric matching between molecular bulk and pore geometry creates strongly different adsorption states for similar molecules. Inference: Vol/lsd_p^3 quantifies steric matching (shape selectivity, E05) as a continuous descriptor; Vol/MW proxies molecular compactness, which modulates how many rotational modes survive confinement (E06). The combination tests whether fit tightness, not just free volume, governs s_ads/s_gas.
descriptor_candidates.falsification_criteria: The descriptor fails if (a) it provides no incremental MAE improvement over the model with the 14 inputs plus log(AV*1e6/Vol), or (b) residual analysis shows no systematic dependence of entropy loss on Vol/lsd_p^3 within any framework family, indicating that cavity-filling fraction does not modulate adsorption entropy independently of occupiable volume.

descriptor_candidates.name: framework_mass_density_d
descriptor_candidates.hypothesis: Hypothesis 4 (framework density-corrected confinement mechanism): For a fixed occupiable volume per molecule, the retained entropy fraction s_ads/s_gas still varies with the framework's mass density and the free-path anisotropy of the pore system. Dense frameworks (high source-scale density) pack confinement sites closer together, increasing wall encounters per unit path length and thus entropy loss; a large lsd_f/lsd_p contrast (long windows between cages) permits partial translational recovery along channels, partially offsetting the loss. The signed combination log(density*AV/Vol) minus (log(lsd_f/lsd_p))^2 encodes this competition and should reduce entropy-loss MAE, particularly distinguishing channel frameworks (TON, MFI) from cage frameworks (FAU, CHA).
descriptor_candidates.rationale: Source evidence: E01 shows absolute entropy loss is framework-specific (TON largest, FAU smallest) even for similar adsorbates; E08 documents framework flexibility/dynamics affecting adsorption behavior, implying framework structure beyond static volume matters; E09 shows confinement geometry (channel vs cage topology) changes molecular mobility. Inference: density (on its source numerical scale, treated as a relative ordering variable) times the per-molecule pore volume measures confinement-site density; the squared log of the lsd_f/lsd_p ratio measures how anisotropic/extended the free path is, which restores some translational entropy. No physical units are assigned to density; only its relative ordering is used.
descriptor_candidates.falsification_criteria: The hypothesis is falsified if (a) the descriptor does not improve MAE of entropy loss/R over the round-1 best model, or (b) the fitted coefficients indicate no distinguishable effect between channel-like and cage-like frameworks in residual analysis (i.e., the lsd_f/lsd_p term contributes nothing), showing framework density and free-path anisotropy carry no entropy information beyond occupiable volume and molecular size.

descriptor_candidates.name: rotational_asymmetry_d
descriptor_candidates.hypothesis: Hypothesis 5 (rotational asymmetry correction to volume confinement): For a given occupiable-volume ratio AV/Vol (Hypothesis 1 mechanism), the retained entropy fraction s_ads/s_gas additionally depends on the molecule's principal-moment asymmetry PMI3/PMI1. Nearly spherical molecules (PMI3/PMI1 ~ 1) lose all three rotational modes almost uniformly in confinement, whereas highly asymmetric molecules (large PMI3/PMI1) retain partial rotation about their smallest-moment axis, especially in channel-like pores. A descriptor combining log(PMI3/PMI1) with a half-weighted negative volume-confinement term should reduce entropy-loss MAE below the round-2 best (0.5484), because rotation loss is multiplicative with the translational confinement already encoded by AV/Vol.
descriptor_candidates.rationale: Source evidence: E01 decomposes gas-phase entropy into translational and rotational fractions per mode and reports framework-specific losses; E06 shows translational and rotational degrees of freedom are reduced by fixed factors when molecules are confined in cavities. Inference: the moment ratio PMI3/PMI1 continuously ranks how many distinct rotational modes a molecule can lose in a pore; subtracting a scaled volume-confinement term makes the descriptor the rotational residual after the known translational effect, testing whether rotational asymmetry carries independent entropy information.
descriptor_candidates.falsification_criteria: Falsified if adding this descriptor does not reduce MAE of entropy loss/R below 0.5484 across cross-validation folds, or if residual analysis shows no systematic PMI3/PMI1 dependence within volume-ratio bins (i.e., rotational asymmetry is fully absorbed by AV/Vol and the raw PMI inputs).

descriptor_candidates.name: wall_contact_fraction_d
descriptor_candidates.hypothesis: Hypothesis 6 (interfacial wall-contact fraction mechanism): Entropy loss scales with the fraction of the adsorbate's configurational phase space within wall-interaction range, proxied by the accessible-surface-area density of the framework (LabuteASA per occupiable volume) multiplied by a molecular size relative to the limiting pore diameter sqrt(Vol/lsd_p). Frameworks with high surface area per pore volume force molecules into frequent wall contact (more frustrated rotations, E01's TON-like behavior), while a molecule that fills a large fraction of the limiting aperture experiences stronger sieving constraints. Unlike the failed round-2 wall-proximity descriptor, this form separates framework surface density from molecular fit, using the unsquared (sqrt) size term to avoid over-weighting extreme values.

retained.name: confined_vol_ratio_d
retained.hypothesis: Hypothesis 1 (occupiable-volume confinement mechanism): The fraction of gas-phase entropy retained upon adsorption, s_ads/s_gas, decreases systematically with the ratio of occupiable pore volume per gram (AV) to molecular volume (Vol), because tighter packing of the guest shape against pore walls suppresses translational freedom. A descriptor built from log(AV/Vol) should reduce entropy-loss MAE relative to a model that already contains the 14 inputs as raw network features, because the network must otherwise learn this multiplicative scaling nonlocally.

retained.name: framework_mass_density_d
retained.hypothesis: Hypothesis 4 (framework density-corrected confinement mechanism): For a fixed occupiable volume per molecule, the retained entropy fraction s_ads/s_gas still varies with the framework's mass density and the free-path anisotropy of the pore system. Dense frameworks (high source-scale density) pack confinement sites closer together, increasing wall encounters per unit path length and thus entropy loss; a large lsd_f/lsd_p contrast (long windows between cages) permits partial translational recovery along channels, partially offsetting the loss. The signed combination log(density*AV/Vol) minus (log(lsd_f/lsd_p))^2 encodes this competition and should reduce entropy-loss MAE, particularly distinguishing channel frameworks (TON, MFI) from cage frameworks (FAU, CHA).
